hints: Work backwards from 3-aminobenzoic acid. The final step reduces a nitro group to an amino group, so what must N contain in place of $\text{NH}_{2}$?
Think about what group must be present in M so that nitration in step 2 puts the nitro group in the 3-position relative to it.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from the amine**
You finish with $3\text{-H}_{2}\text{N-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$. The classic way to make an aromatic amine is to reduce an aromatic nitro compound. So N must be the same skeleton but with $\text{NO}_{2}$ where the $\text{NH}_{2}$ now is. That gives 3-nitrobenzoic acid.

Work back one more step to M**
N was made by nitration of M. N already contains $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ and $\text{NO}_{2}$. Nitration adds $\text{NO}_{2}$, so M must already contain the $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ group. M is therefore benzoic acid, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.

Check the directing effect makes sense**
$\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ is a deactivating meta-director. Nitration of benzoic acid therefore gives the 3-nitro isomer as the major product, exactly what you need for 3-aminobenzoic acid after reduction. This confirms the order: oxidise first, then nitrate.

Final answer: M is benzoic acid, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.
N is 3-nitrobenzoic acid, $3\text{-O}_{2}\text{N-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$ with $\text{NO}_{2}$ meta to $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.

hints: Recall the reagent that oxidises an alkyl side chain on benzene completely to $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, even though the benzene ring itself survives.
Recall the standard pair of concentrated acids used to generate the nitronium ion $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$ for electrophilic substitution.
Recall the metal plus concentrated acid combination, with heat, that reduces $\text{Ar-NO}_{2}$ to $\text{Ar-NH}_{2}$ without affecting $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1, methyl to carboxylic acid**
You need $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{3}$ to $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. This is vigorous side chain oxidation. Use hot concentrated $\text{KMnO}_{4}$, alkaline then acid work up. The benzene ring is stable to this oxidation, only the alkyl side chain is oxidised.

Step 2, nitration**
You need benzoic acid to 3-nitrobenzoic acid. This is electrophilic nitration. Use a nitrating mixture of concentrated $\text{HNO}_{3}$ plus concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$. The $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ acts as acid to form the electrophile: $$\text{HNO}_{3} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} \rightarrow \text{NO}_{2}^{+} + 2\text{HSO}_{4}^{-} + \text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+}$$

Step 3, nitro to amine**
You need $\text{Ar-NO}_{2}$ to $\text{Ar-NH}_{2}$. This is reduction. Use tin and concentrated $\text{HCl}$ with heat, followed by alkali to liberate the free amine. This is the standard non-catalytic method that leaves $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ unchanged.

Final answer: step 1: hot $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ / alkaline $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$, heat, then acidify.
step 2: conc. $\text{HNO}_{3}$ and conc. $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$, heat below $55^{\circ}\text{C}$.
step 3: Sn and conc. $\text{HCl}$, heat.

hints: Two serine molecules $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ can condense with loss of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. What two different functional group pairings can lose water?
For the amide isomer, join $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ of one serine to $\text{NH}_{2}$ of the other to make $\text{CONH}$.
For the ester isomer, join $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ of one serine to the side chain $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ of the other to make $\text{COO}$.
walkthrough:
See serine has three reactive groups**
Serine is $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. It has an alcohol $\text{OH}$, an amine $\text{NH}_{2}$ and a carboxylic acid $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. When two molecules condense with loss of one $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, the acid can react with either the amine or the alcohol.

Build the amide linkage**
Acid plus amine gives amide plus water: $$\text{RCO}_{2}\text{H} + \text{H}_{2}\text{N-R'} \rightarrow \text{RCONH-R'} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ Using the alpha $\text{NH}_{2}$ gives the dipeptide $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CONHCH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. You must display the $\text{C(=O)-NH}$ atoms.

Build the ester linkage**
Acid plus alcohol gives ester plus water: $$\text{RCO}_{2}\text{H} + \text{HO-R'} \rightarrow \text{RCOOR'} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ Using the side chain $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ gives $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COOCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. You must display the $\text{C(=O)-O}$ atoms.

Final answer: amide (dipeptide): $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CONHCH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ with $\text{CO-NH}$ linkage displayed.
ester: $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COOCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ with $\text{CO-O}$ linkage displayed.

hints: Add the formulas of serine $(\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{7}\text{NO}_{3})$ and lysine $(\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{14}\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{2})$ then subtract $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ for one condensation, and count how many different $\text{NH}_{2}$ and $\text{OH}$ pairings are possible.
walkthrough:
Combine formulas then subtract water**
Serine $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{7}\text{NO}_{3}$ plus lysine $\text{H}_{2}\text{N(CH}_{2}\text{)}_{4}\text{CH(NH}_{2}\text{)CO}_{2}\text{H}$, which is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{14}\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{2}$, gives $\text{C}_{9}\text{H}_{21}\text{N}_{3}\text{O}_{5}$. Lose one $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ in condensation: $$\text{C}_{9}\text{H}_{21}\text{N}_{3}\text{O}_{5} - \text{H}_{2}\text{O} = \text{C}_{9}\text{H}_{19}\text{N}_{3}\text{O}_{4}$$ Lysine has two different $\text{NH}_{2}$ groups (alpha and side chain) and serine offers both $\text{NH}_{2}$ and $\text{OH}$ for reaction with $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, plus the reverse acid amine pairing, giving 4 distinct amide and ester structural isomers.
Final answer: molecular formula $\text{C}_{9}\text{H}_{19}\text{N}_{3}\text{O}_{4}$; number of structural isomers formed = 4.

hints: A chiral carbon has four different groups attached. Look along the glutathione backbone for $\text{CH}$ carbons bonded to $\text{NH}_{2}$ or $\text{NH}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{C=O}$ and a different carbon side chain.
walkthrough:
Test each carbon for four different groups**
The left $\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})$ is bonded to $\text{NH}_{2}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}$, so it is chiral. The middle $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{SH})$ is bonded to $\text{NH}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{SH}$, so it is also chiral. The $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups and the glycine $\text{CH}_{2}$ have two H atoms, so they are not chiral.

Final answer: Mark * on the $\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})$ carbon of the glutamic acid residue and on the $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{SH})$ carbon of the cysteine residue: $\text{HO}_{2}\text{CCH}(\text{NH}_{2}*)\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CONHCH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{SH}*)\text{CONHCH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.

hints: Acid hydrolysis breaks every $\text{CONH}$ peptide bond by adding water across it, so a tripeptide gives three separate amino acids.
Split glutathione at the two $\text{CO-NH}$ links and complete each fragment with $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ on the carbonyl side and $\text{NH}_{2}$ on the nitrogen side.
walkthrough:
Locate the peptide bonds to cleave**
Glutathione has two amide links: $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-C(=O)-NH-CH}$ and $\text{CH-C(=O)-NH-CH}_{2}$. Hydrolysis is the reverse of condensation: $$\text{RCONH-R'} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{RCO}_{2}\text{H} + \text{R'NH}_{2}$$

Write the three fragments**
Breaking both links restores the original monomers: glutamic acid $\text{HO}_{2}\text{CCH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, cysteine $\text{H}_{2}\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{SH})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, and glycine $\text{H}_{2}\text{NCH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.

Final answer: $\text{HO}_{2}\text{CCH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ (glutamic acid) and $\text{H}_{2}\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{SH})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ (cysteine) and $\text{H}_{2}\text{NCH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ (glycine).

hints: Look at the $\text{OH}$, $\text{NH}$, $\text{C=O}$, $\text{SH}$ and $\text{NH}_{2}$ groups in glutathione and think about what type of intermolecular attraction they can form with water molecules.
walkthrough:
Link polar groups to solubility**
Water is a hydrogen bond donor and acceptor. Glutathione is loaded with $\text{O-H}$, $\text{N-H}$, $\text{C=O}$ and amine groups that can donate or accept hydrogen bonds to water. These solute water hydrogen bonds release enough energy to overcome glutathione glutathione attractions, so it dissolves well.
Final answer: Glutathione can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules via its $\text{-OH}$, $\text{-NH-}$, $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$ and $\text{-NH}_{2}$ groups.
